pull.title: KAFKA-20999: [2/N] Add rack-aware standby task assignment to sticky assignor
pull.body:
Second part of rack-aware standby placement for streams groups. It wires
RackAwareStandbyPicker (#23790) into StickyTaskAssignor. Without
rack.aware.assignment.tags, the assignment is unchanged.

Rack diversity ranks above stickiness, so standbys are now assigned in
four steps:
1. Get the best condition for rack awareness, and traverse all the
previous member, assignor it back to a previous member if it satisfy the
condition
2. Assignor it to the least-loaded process that satisfy the best
condtiion
3. Assignor it back to previous member if it has room
4. Assignor it to least-loaded process with no rack constrain

A process has room while one of its members is below the per-member
quota on active plus standby tasks; a least-loaded pick goes to that
member. After each placement, the assignor reports the change to the
picker with updated(), or updatedAll() when the quota drops, since a
lower quota can take the room of any process.

StreamsAssignorBenchmark gets a rackAwareTags parameter with five tag
layouts, two of them with one host per process, and standbyReplicas=2.

Reviewers: Lucas Brutschy <lbrutschy@confluent.io>

review_comments.body: leastLoadedMemberWithRoom scans every member of the process, and it's called here for every candidate on every pickCandidates() filter pass (could be more than once per standby, if a key gets given up), then again at placement time for the winner. With membersPerProcess around 50 like the benchmark uses, that's a lot of repeat scanning. Could we cache the least-loaded-member-with-room per process and only invalidate it when that process actually gets a placement?

This prev-active -> prev-standby-least-loaded -> least-loaded tie-break is the same one already written for the tag-blind path a bit above. Worth pulling into a shared helper so the two passes can't drift apart if the tie-break rule ever changes.
sure, I will update it thanks.
sounds good, I will turn it into a helper.

This adds a second cache for "least loaded member" (a scalar recomputed by a full scan) alongside membersByLoad, the existing PriorityQueue that already answers this. Now there are two mechanisms for the same thing that have to stay in sync, and the new one is O(n) per miss vs O(log n) for the queue. Was membersByLoad not sufficient here, or is this meant to replace it?

assignStandby now runs four phases (rack-aware-sticky, rack-aware-least-loaded, tag-blind-sticky, tag-blind-least-loaded) with three bookkeeping collections (currentStandbys, rackAwareStandbys, rackNonSticky) threaded through one long method. The per-task diversity logic got its own abstraction in RackAwareStandbyPicker; would it help readability to pull the phase ordering/precedence out into something similar, rather than following it inline here?

leastLoaded() scans every candidate group linearly, comparing PQ heads one by one. Since each ProcessGroup already exposes an ordered least-loaded-with-room head, a small merge-heap over the group heads would make this O(log #groups) instead of O(#groups). Minor at today's group counts, but it's basically free given the structure already here.
Looks like this is addressed in the latest push - ProcessState now caches leastLoadedMember(), invalidated on task add. Thanks!
This got factored out in the latest push too - both paths now go through one findPrevMemberForStandby(..., allowed) helper. Nice.

sounds good, I have moved steps 1 and 2 into assignRackAwareStandbys, and assignStandby now only orders   
the rack-aware and tag-blind steps, and steps 3–4 match trunk apart from the start index.

it was originally used to handle the problem of we put task back to sticky member, then in the least-loaded stage, it won't be updated. But I realized I can just recored what has been changed and check if the least-loaded member's room has expired. I have updated it now. Thanks for pointing it out

review_comments.body:
**Why ids instead of tag strings**

The picker turns each tag value into a small number once, up front. With `rack.aware.assignment.tags=cluster,zone`:

| group | cluster | zone | ids |
|---|---|---|---|
| G1 | c1 | z1 | [0, 0] |
| G2 | c2 | z2 | [1, 1] |
| G3 | c1 | z3 | [0, 2] |

"Is this value already used by the task?" then becomes an array lookup instead of a string lookup in a set:

```java
// before
!usedTagValues.get(keyIndex).contains(candidate.clientTags.get(tagKeys.get(keyIndex)))
// after
!usedTagValues[keyIndex][candidate.valueIds[keyIndex]]
```

This check runs for every candidate on every pick, so it's the hot path. We only ever compared tags for equality, and ids are equal exactly when the strings are, so the behavior is the same.

cause for rack-aware pick, the processes for leastLoaded() are those process also satisfy rack-diverse condition. So it won't save that much of time since each time the input are different. Also, since we are using group, the O(#surviver_groups) should be small enough
A lot of this logic (the tag grouping) could/should be reused in the balanced assignor. Could we move it to a place where the implementation can be shared?
That seems like a fairly optimistic case. what happens if we increase the number of groups?

make sense, I have moved it to a package-private IdenticalTagGroups

next to RackAwareStandbyPicker. It holds the grouping by tag values and the lazy least-loaded queue of each group, and takes the assignor's load function and room check as parameters.
i can add a new tag, so the tags will be "cluster,zone,rack", and also check what if each process all have different tags.

Step 2 still checks the previous members first, because a pick can have looser conditions in step 2 than it had in step 1.

For example, with rack.aware.assignment.tags = `zone,cluster`: the task's active is on M0 (zone1, cluster2) and its previous standby was on M1 (zone1, cluster1). No process is in both a new zone and a new cluster, so in step 1 the pick keeps only [zone], and its only candidate is M3 (zone2, cluster2). M1 is not a candidate, so step 1 leaves this standby to step 2.

By the time step 2 picks for the task, standbys of other tasks have filled M3. No process with room is in a new zone anymore, so the pick falls back to [cluster], and M1 is a candidate again, together with M4 (zone1, cluster3). The standby should go back to M1, which already has the state, rather than to M4, even if M4 is less loaded.

The same can happen within one task: once step 2 places a standby, the next pick for that task may drop a key whose values are now all used, and a previous member can become a candidate.
while the metric in rack aware basically the same, the stickiness increased

If the prev standby member picked here is already at quota, this returns null even when another prev standby member on a candidate process is still below quota. `findPrevMemberWithLeastLoad` never looks at the member quota, and only replaces its pick when both process and member load are strictly lower. In step 1 this makes `placeRackAwareStandbys` return early, so the standby goes cold in step 2.

Repro (fails with `expected: <[m2]> but was: <[m1b]>`):
```java
final Map<String, MemberMetadataAndStateImpl> members = mkMap(
    mkEntry("a0", createTaggedMemberMetadata("P0", Map.of("rack", "A"), Map.of("s", Set.of(0)), Map.of())),
    mkEntry("m1", createTaggedMemberMetadataWithOffsets("P1", Map.of("rack", "B"), Map.of("s", Set.of(1)), Map.of("s", Set.of(4, 0)), Map.of("s", Map.of(0, 9000L)))),
    mkEntry("m1b", createTaggedMemberMetadata("P1", Map.of("rack", "B"), Map.of("s", Set.of(2)), Map.of())),
    mkEntry("m2", createTaggedMemberMetadataWithOffsets("P2", Map.of("rack", "C"), Map.of("s", Set.of(3)), Map.of("s", Set.of(0)), Map.of("s", Map.of(0, 100L)))),
    mkEntry("m2b", createTaggedMemberMetadata("P2", Map.of("rack", "C"), Map.of("s", Set.of(4)), Map.of("s", Set.of(1))))
);
final GroupAssignment result = assignor.assign(
    new GroupSpecImpl(members, AssignmentConfigsImpl.DEFAULT.withNumStandbyReplicas(1).withRackAwareAssignmentTags(List.of("rack"))),
    new TopologyDescriberImpl(5, true, List.of("s")));
assertEquals(Set.of("m2"), standbyHolders(result, "s", 0));
```

The tag-blind loop already had this before the PR, but there it just fell through to least-loaded. Checking `hasUnfulfilledTaskQuota` inside `findPrevMemberWithLeastLoad` (e.g. as part of the predicate) would fix both.

Here's a case where this trade-off costs a standby move without buying any diversity: zone tag, 1 standby, 4 tasks, A/B/C in z1 and D alone in z2 (A: active 1, standby 0; B: active 0; C: active 3; D: active 2). Task 3's standby fills D. Task 2's standby can go to A, B or C at equal load and takes A, which fills it. Task 0's prev standby on A is lost and it ends up cold on C, although B or C would have served task 2 just as well.

Would it be worth breaking step-2 ties away from processes that a not-yet-placed prev standby holder still needs? Not a blocker, since diversity is never lost.

nit: none of the new tests covers a sticky pick where the prev member is at quota but another member of its process still has room, so `isCandidate` passes but `hasUnfulfilledTaskQuota` fails. Would be good to have one, given the issue in `findPrevMemberForStandby`.

This grows the matrix from 256 to 1920 combinations, and roughly half of them measure the same thing: BALANCED never reads the tags, and STICKY with `standbyReplicas=0` skips the standby path. Maybe add a note like the one for `reportedOffsets`, or narrow the defaults?

nit: this is an assumption rather than a guarantee. After an unclean shutdown with changed `client.tag.*`, the old members (same processId from the state dir) can stay in the group with the old tags until session timeout, and then which tags win depends on `memberIds()` order. The classic assignor does the same, so fine to keep, but maybe phrase the comment as an assumption.
Minor: this and `processIdToClientTags` are only read on the rack-aware path. Could skip filling them when there are no tags or no standbys.
nit: could you add parentheses here, or split it into two `continue` checks? It's correct by precedence but easy to misread.

### Testbed results
